note: These texts are UNOFFICIAL explanatory translations of the Turkish summaries, which are themselves based on official Diyanet sources. They are not official English fatwas or publications of the Diyanet.

articles.title: What is Islam?
articles.summary: Islam is the faith built on believing in the oneness of God and submitting to Him wholeheartedly.

sections.text: The word Islam literally means "to submit, to be at peace". As a term it refers to believing in the oneness of God, willingly following the guidance He revealed, and finding peace through that trust.
According to Islamic belief, God sent prophets and scriptures to humanity throughout history. The final link in this chain is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the Qur'an revealed to him.
Islam is not only a set of beliefs; it is an integrated way of life that also includes worship and character.
A person becomes Muslim by accepting the declaration of faith sincerely and saying it. Knowledge and practice are then learned gradually and patiently; everyone starts from a different point.
If you want to learn one thing today, you could begin by reading the meaning of the declaration of faith.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), İkinci Bölüm II. İSLAM, s. 83
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde İslam, 'Hz. Muhammed'in Allah tarafından getirdiği kesin olarak bilinen şeyleri kalp ile tasdik edip, bunlardan iş ve davranışla ilgili olanları yapmak' şeklinde tanımlanır; makaledeki tanım bu bölüme dayanır.

articles.title: The articles of faith
articles.summary: The essentials of belief are gathered under six headings, known together as the "Amantu".

sections.text: Faith means affirming with the heart and expressing with the tongue. The essentials of Islamic belief are traditionally summarised under six headings.

items: Belief in God: that He exists, is one and without equal.
Belief in His angels: beings created from light who follow His command.
Belief in His scriptures: the revelations sent to His prophets.
Belief in His prophets: the messengers sent to humanity.
Belief in the Hereafter: life after death and the reckoning.
Belief in destiny, that both good and hardship occur within God's knowledge and will.

sections.text: These six essentials form one inseparable whole; one is not accepted while another is rejected.
Learning the articles of faith is not merely memorisation. Reflecting on the meaning of each one makes belief more conscious.
Choose one of the six and simply reflect on its meaning today.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Birinci Bölüm IV. İMAN, F) İman Esasları, s. 41
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde iman esaslarının altı olduğu ve Âmentü cümlesinde toplandığı açıkça belirtilir; makaledeki altı madde bu bölümle birebir örtüşür.

articles.title: The pillars of Islam
articles.summary: The five foundations: the declaration of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting, and pilgrimage for those able.

sections.text: The core acts of worship in Islam are summarised under five headings. They are known as the pillars and form the main framework of a Muslim's life.

items: Declaring the testimony of faith.
Performing the prayer.
Giving zakat (for those who own wealth above the threshold).
Fasting in the month of Ramadan.
Performing hajj once in a lifetime for those who are able.

sections.text: Zakat and hajj are not obligatory on everyone; they apply to those who meet specific means and conditions.
These acts are not simply a checklist of duties. Each one draws a person closer to God and trains patience and generosity.
If you do not yet pray regularly, you could pick one prayer time and build consistency there first.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), İkinci Bölüm II. İSLAM, A) İslam'ın Şartları, s. 84
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde 'İslam beş temel üzerine kurulmuştur' rivayeti ve beş şart sayılır; makaledeki beş madde bununla örtüşür.

articles.title: The declaration of faith
articles.summary: The sentence by which a person expresses faith, and what it means.

sections.text: The declaration of faith is the sentence by which a person states their belief. It is transliterated as: "Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan abduhu wa rasuluh."
It means: "I bear witness that there is no deity but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger."
The sentence expresses two things together: the oneness of God and the prophethood of Muhammad. For it to be meaningful, it must be accepted sincerely in the heart.
A person who says this with belief becomes Muslim. Learning worship and religious knowledge afterwards is a gradual process that moves at each person's own pace.
Read the sentence slowly and try to express what each part means in your own words.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), IV. İMAN, A) Kelime-i Tevhid ve Kelime-i Şahadet, s. 39
verification.evidenceSummary: Şehadet cümlesinin metni ve 'kalpteki imanın dil ile ifadesi' tanımı eserde yer alır; makaledeki okunuş ve anlam bununla örtüşür.

articles.title: How is wudu performed?
articles.summary: The step-by-step practice and order of ablution.

sections.text: Wudu is the state of purity required for prayer and certain other acts of worship. The order below summarises the common practice; the strictly obligatory parts are covered in a separate topic.

items: Form the intention for wudu and say the basmala.
Wash your hands up to the wrists three times, including between the fingers.
Rinse your mouth three times using your right hand.
Draw water into your nose three times and clean it with your left hand.
Wash your face three times, from the hairline to below the chin.
Wash your right then left arm, including the elbows, three times each.
Wet your hands and wipe over your head.
Wipe your ears and then your neck.
Wash your right then left foot, including the ankles, three times each.

sections.text: Washing means the whole limb becomes wet. No dry spot should remain where water has not reached.
Read the steps through slowly once, then try it; memorising comes naturally with time.
This summary is based on the section on wudu in the Diyanet İslam İlmihali; it is not a direct quotation from that work.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), V. ABDEST, F) Abdest Nasıl Alınır?, s. 105-107
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde abdestin uygulanış sırası (kolların sıvanması, kıbleye dönülmesi, elleri/ağzı/burnu/yüzü/kolları yıkama, başın meshi, ayakların yıkanması) adım adım anlatılır; makaledeki adımlar bu bölümle örtüşür.

articles.title: The obligatory parts of wudu
articles.summary: The parts that must be performed for ablution to be valid.

sections.text: The obligatory parts of wudu are those that must be performed for the ablution to be valid. The remaining practices fall under recommended acts and etiquette.

items: Washing the face once.
Washing the arms including the elbows once.
Wiping one quarter of the head.
Washing the feet including the ankles once.

sections.text: If one obligatory part is left out, the wudu is incomplete; it is completed by washing the missed limb.
The elbows and the ankles are the most commonly missed areas — pay attention to those two.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), V. ABDEST, B) Abdestin Farzları, s. 98-99
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde 'abdestin farzları dörttür' denilerek yüzü yıkamak, kolları dirseklerle yıkamak, başın dörtte birini meshetmek ve ayakları topuklarla yıkamak sayılır; makaledeki dört madde bununla birebir örtüşür.

articles.title: What invalidates wudu
articles.summary: The main situations that require renewing ablution.

sections.text: Certain situations end the state of wudu and require it to be renewed before worship. The main ones are:

items: Relieving oneself or passing wind.
Blood, pus or similar discharge leaving the body and spreading.
Vomiting a mouthful.
Fainting, intoxication, or temporary loss of awareness.
Falling into deep sleep while lying down or leaning against something.
Laughing audibly during the prayer.

sections.text: These items largely follow the Hanafi school. For example, blood leaving the body invalidating wudu is the Hanafi position; in the Shafi'i school it does not, while certain forms of skin contact are treated differently. Such differences should be known rather than hidden.
When in doubt, the previously certain state prevails: if you are not sure your wudu broke, you are considered to still have it.
If you want to follow the practice of your own school, read the relevant section of a handbook that follows that position.

articles.differenceNote: What invalidates wudu differs between the schools of law.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), V. ABDEST, I) Abdesti Bozan Şeyler, s. 110 (Şâfiî farkı: 25 numaralı dipnot)
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde abdesti bozan sekiz hâl sayılır ve 25 numaralı dipnotta Şâfiîlere göre ön/arka dışındaki kanın abdesti bozmadığı belirtilir; makaledeki liste ve mezhep farkı notu bu bölümle desteklenir.

articles.title: How is ghusl performed?
articles.summary: The obligatory parts and practice of the full ritual washing.

sections.text: Ghusl is the state of purity achieved by washing the entire body.

items: Form the intention and say the basmala.
Wash your hands and clean any impurity on the body.
Perform wudu.
Rinse your mouth thoroughly.
Draw water into your nose and clean it.
Pour water over your head, then your right and left shoulder, washing the whole body.
Make sure no part of the body remains dry.

sections.text: According to the Hanafi school the obligatory parts of ghusl are three: rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, and washing the entire body.
The roots of the hair and behind the ears are the spots water most often fails to reach.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VII. GUSÜL, C) Guslün Farzları ve G) Gusül Nasıl Yapılır?, s. 121-122
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde guslün farzlarının üç olduğu (mazmaza, istinşak, bütün bedeni yıkamak) ve uygulanış sırası açıklanır; makaledeki farzlar ve adımlar bu bölümlerle örtüşür.

articles.title: What is tayammum?
articles.summary: The form of purification used when water is unavailable or cannot be used.

sections.text: Tayammum is the purification performed with clean earth or an earthen surface when water is unavailable or cannot be used, for example due to health reasons.

items: Form the intention for tayammum.
Strike both hands on clean earth or an earthen surface.
Wipe your face with your hands.
Strike the surface a second time.
Wipe your arms including the elbows.

sections.text: Tayammum can take the place of both wudu and ghusl. Its ruling ends once water becomes available or usable again.
Being unable to use water for health reasons is a personal situation. When deciding for your own case it is appropriate to consult both your doctor and a qualified religious official.

articles.guidanceMessage: For special circumstances related to health, you can consult a qualified religious official or the High Board of Religious Affairs.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VI. TEYEMMÜM, C) Teyemmümün Farzları ve E) Teyemmüm Nasıl Yapılır?, s. 118
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde teyemmümün farzlarının iki olduğu (niyet ve iki vuruşla yüz/kolların meshi) ve uygulanışı açıklanır; makaledeki adımlar bununla örtüşür.

articles.title: Preparing for prayer
articles.summary: The conditions to be met before beginning the prayer.

sections.text: For the prayer to be valid, certain conditions must be met before it begins. These are known as the conditions outside the prayer itself.

items: Having wudu (or ghusl where required).
Cleanliness of the body, clothing and the place of prayer.
Covering the parts of the body that must be covered.
Facing the qibla.
The time of the prayer having begun.
Forming the intention for the prayer to be performed.

sections.text: Intention is the turning of the heart; it does not require long sentences spoken aloud.
Although the conditions may look complex, most are already met in daily life. Over time these steps become an effortless habit.
Preparing your prayer space in advance makes starting noticeably easier.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VIII. NAMAZ, F) Namazın Farzları / a) Namazın Şartları, s. 144
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde namazın dışındaki altı şart (hadesten ve necasetten taharet, setr-i avret, istikbal-i kıble, vakit, niyet) sayılır; makaledeki kontrol listesi bununla örtüşür.

articles.title: The five daily prayers
articles.summary: The five prayer times and the number of obligatory units in each.

sections.text: The five daily prayers are obligatory upon every Muslim who has reached maturity and is of sound mind. Each prayer has its own time window.

items: Fajr: 2 obligatory units.
Dhuhr: 4 obligatory units.
Asr: 4 obligatory units.
Maghrib: 3 obligatory units.
Isha: 4 obligatory units.

sections.text: The numbers above are only the obligatory units. Recommended prayers attached to each time are performed separately.
Prayer times are determined by the position of the sun, so they vary by location and season. You can see the times calculated for your location in the Prayer tab of this app.
If praying regularly feels difficult, you can aim to make just one prayer time consistent first.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VIII. NAMAZ, İ) Beş Vakit Namazın Kılınışı, s. 152-160
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde her vaktin rekât dağılımı açıkça verilir: öğle ve yatsı onar rekâttan dördü farz, ikindi sekiz rekâttan dördü farz, akşam beş rekâttan üçü farz, sabahın farzı iki rekâttır; makaledeki farz sayıları bunlarla örtüşür.

articles.title: The main parts of the prayer
articles.summary: The building blocks of a unit: standing, recitation, bowing, prostration and sitting.

sections.text: The prayer is made up of repeating units. Within each unit, specific parts are carried out in order.

items: Opening takbir: beginning the prayer by saying "Allahu akbar".
Standing.
Recitation from the Qur'an.
Bowing, with the hands on the knees.
Prostration, with the forehead, nose, hands, knees and toes touching the ground (twice in each unit).
The final sitting at the end of the prayer.

sections.text: Coming to stillness for a moment in each part is the basis of praying calmly; it is not rushed.
Naming each part as you learn makes the flow of the prayer easier to remember.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VIII. NAMAZ, F/b) Namazın Rükünleri, s. 145-147
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde namazın rükünleri iftitah tekbiri, kıyam, kıraat, rükû, secde ve ka'de-i ahire olarak sayılır; makaledeki bölümler bu sıralamayla örtüşür.

articles.title: What is the Qur'an?
articles.summary: The definition, structure and preservation of the Qur'an.

sections.text: The Qur'an is the divine scripture revealed by God to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and transmitted without interruption from generation to generation.
The Qur'an consists of 114 chapters. Chapters are made up of verses, and the complete text gathered between two covers is called a mushaf.
It was revealed in parts over roughly twenty-three years, in response to events and needs. The revelation was preserved both in writing and through memorisation.
The Qur'an is originally in Arabic. Texts in other languages are called translations of meaning; they are an effort to convey the meaning and do not take the place of the Qur'an itself.
You can begin reading the original Arabic text together with its translation in the Quran tab of this app.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Kitaplara İman — Kur'an-ı Kerim'in Nazil Oluşu ve Özellikleri, s. 54-58
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde Kur'an'ın vahiy yoluyla indirildiği, tevatür yoluyla nakledildiği, mushaf hâlinde yazıldığı ve 114 sureden oluştuğu belirtilir; makaledeki tanım ve yapı bilgisi bu bölümlere dayanır.

articles.title: What does learning the Qur'an mean?
articles.summary: According to the İslam İlmihali, learning the Qur'an means both learning to read it and working to understand its meaning. The same section states that tajwid must also be learned in order to read it without error.

sections.text: Under the heading "Our duties towards the Qur'an", the İslam İlmihali lists one of those duties as "learning the Qur'an".
The source defines that learning as follows: learning the Qur'an means learning to read it and working to understand its meaning.
So reading and understanding are presented in the source not as two separate tasks, but as two sides of the same learning.

The same section states that tajwid must also be learned in order to read the Qur'an without error. In the source tajwid appears not as a subject outside learning the Qur'an, but as part of that learning.

This article conveys the source's definition. It does not propose a programme, a duration, a pace or a daily amount of reading; for questions about your own path of learning you may consult the competent official authority or a trusted teacher.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Kur'an-ı Kerim'e Karşı Görevlerimiz — b) Kur'an-ı Kerim'i Öğrenmek, s. 58
verification.evidenceSummary: s. 58'deki "Kur'an-ı Kerim'e Karşı Görevlerimiz" başlığının (b) maddesi "Kur'an-ı Kerim'i öğrenmek"tir. Makale yalnız bu iki cümleye dayanır; aynı sayfadaki övgü/fazilet ifadeleri, hadis ve namazla ilgili hüküm cümlesi makaleye alınmamıştır.

articles.title: The etiquette of supplication
articles.summary: What supplication means and the attitudes that beautify it.

sections.text: Supplication is a servant turning to God and presenting their state. It is not bound to a particular time, place or language; everyone may supplicate in their own tongue.

items: Beginning by praising God.
Sending blessings upon the Prophet.
Asking sincerely and with hope.
Continuing to supplicate with persistence and patience.
Leaving the answer to God's wisdom.

sections.text: Rather than thinking a supplication went unanswered, the understanding is that its answer comes at the most fitting time and in the most fitting form.
Supplication is not only for hard times. Praying in peaceful moments too keeps the bond between servant and God continuous.
Make a short supplication in your own words today; no memorised phrase is required.

verification.blocker: Hadislerle İslam gövdesi okunamadı; ilmihalde dua adabı için kesin bölüm/sayfa eşleştirilemedi.

articles.title: Repentance and hope
articles.summary: Turning back from a mistake, and never despairing of God's mercy.

sections.text: Repentance is feeling regret for a mistake and turning back to God. In Islamic belief, no person is outside the reach of mercy, however many mistakes they have made.

items: Recognising the mistake and feeling regret.
Leaving that behaviour.
Sincerely intending not to return to it.
Making amends where the rights of another person are involved.

sections.text: Repentance is not a one-time act. When a mistake happens again, it is always possible to repent again.
Despair is one of the heaviest burdens because it prevents a person from beginning again. Yet the door of return is always open, and it is never considered too late.
Rather than dwelling at length on the past, you could choose one small good step for today.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Nafile Namazlar, 7. Tevbe Namazı, s. 224
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde günah işleyen kimsenin hemen pişman olup tevbe etmesi, günahtan derhal vazgeçmesi ve samimi biçimde bağışlanma dilemesi gerektiği belirtilir; makaledeki tevbe adımları bu bölüme dayanır.

articles.title: The two kinds of purity
articles.summary: Purity in Islam has two aspects: removing ritual impurity and removing physical impurity.

sections.text: Purity in Islam is treated under two headings. The first is removing the ritual state that prevents worship; the second is removing physical impurity from the body, clothing or place of prayer.

items: Removing ritual impurity: purifying from the state that prevents worship.
Removing physical impurity: cleaning the body, clothing and place of prayer.

sections.text: Ritual impurity is of two degrees: the lesser is the state of being without wudu and is removed by wudu; the greater requires ghusl.
When water is unavailable or cannot be used, tayammum takes the place of wudu and ghusl.
Before preparing for prayer, consider which kind of purification is needed: wudu or ghusl?

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), III. TEMİZLİK, B) Temizliğin Çeşitleri, s. 90-91
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde temizliğin hadesten taharet ve necasetten taharet olmak üzere iki türlü olduğu, hadesin küçük ve büyük diye ikiye ayrıldığı belirtilir.

articles.title: What is najasah?
articles.summary: For the prayer to be valid, the body, clothing and place of prayer must be free of physical impurity.

sections.text: What is religiously considered impure is called najasah, and removing it is called purification from najasah. For the prayer to be valid, the body, clothing and place of prayer must be clean.

items: Heavy impurity: substances classed as the graver kind.
Light impurity: substances classed as the lighter kind.

sections.text: The work treats more than roughly one dirham (about 2.08 g) of solid heavy impurity, or more than a palm's width of the liquid kind, as preventing the prayer.
Amounts below these do not invalidate the prayer, though cleaning them is still appropriate.
If there is a visible stain on your clothing before prayer, clean it before you begin.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), III. TEMİZLİK, B/2) Necasetten Taharet, s. 91

articles.title: The recommended acts of wudu
articles.summary: Practices beyond the obligatory parts that complete and beautify the ablution.

sections.text: Practices outside the obligatory parts of wudu fall under recommended acts and etiquette. They make the ablution complete and excellent.

items: Washing the hands to the wrists at the start.
Beginning with the basmala.
Rinsing the mouth and nose.
Washing each limb three times.
Starting from the right and keeping the order.
Passing the fingers between one another.

sections.text: The work states there are no wajib acts in wudu; what lies beyond the obligatory parts is recommended or etiquette.
Leaving a recommended act does not invalidate the wudu, but it lessens its completeness.
Try consciously observing just one recommended act the next time you make wudu.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), V. ABDEST, C) Abdestin Sünnetleri, s. 101-104
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde abdestin başlıca sünnetleri sıralanır ve abdestte vacip bulunmadığı belirtilir; makaledeki maddeler bu bölümden özetlenmiştir.

articles.title: Wiping over leather socks
articles.summary: Wiping over footwear that meets certain conditions is permitted in place of washing the feet.

sections.text: Khuff is footwear covering the feet including the ankles. During wudu it is permitted to wipe over them instead of washing the feet, and this is noted as one of the eases of the religion.

items: They must be put on after a wudu in which the feet were washed.
They must cover the feet including the ankles.
They must be durable enough for a farsakh (about twelve thousand paces) of walking.

sections.text: The work lists seven conditions in total for wiping to be valid; those above are the principal ones.
Wiping is valid for a limited period; once it ends, the footwear is removed and the feet washed.
If you are considering using khuff, first learn its conditions and time limit from the relevant section.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), V. ABDEST, K) Mestler Üzerine Meshetmek, s. 112-114
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde mestin tanımı, mesh edilebilmesi için gereken yedi şart ve meshin müddeti açıklanır; makaledeki şartlar bu bölümden özetlenmiştir.

articles.title: When ghusl becomes necessary
articles.summary: In certain states wudu is not sufficient and washing the whole body is required.

sections.text: In some states wudu is not sufficient, and washing the entire body — ghusl — becomes necessary.

items: Entering the state of janabah.
The ending of menstruation for women.
The ending of postnatal bleeding.

sections.text: A person in a state requiring ghusl does not pray until they have performed it.
These matters can involve details specific to a person's own situation; when in doubt it is appropriate to consult a qualified religious official.
You can learn the obligatory parts and method of ghusl from the related topic.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VII. GUSÜL, B) Gusül Yapmayı Gerektiren Hâller, s. 120-121

articles.title: The prayer times
articles.summary: Each of the five obligatory prayers has a defined beginning and end.

sections.text: There are five obligatory prayers each day, and each has its own defined time. Performing a prayer within its own time is a condition of its validity.
It is not permitted to pray before a time has begun, and delaying a prayer past its time without a valid excuse is a serious matter.
The time of the dawn prayer begins with the true dawn spreading along the horizon and lasts until sunrise. This moment is also the start of the fast.
The vertical light that appears and then fades before it is called the false dawn and is not taken as the start of the time. The noon prayer begins when the sun passes its zenith.
You can see the times calculated for your location in the Prayer tab of this app.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), VIII. NAMAZ, C) Namaz Vakitleri, s. 134-137
verification.evidenceSummary: Eserde günde beş farz namaz bulunduğu, her birinin belirli vakti olduğu ve sabah vaktinin fecr-i sadıkla başlayıp güneşin doğuşuna kadar sürdüğü açıklanır; makaledeki vakit tanımları bu bölüme dayanır.

articles.title: The obligatory parts of the prayer
articles.summary: The prayer has twelve obligatory parts: six conditions before it and six pillars within it.

sections.text: The obligatory parts required for the prayer to be valid fall into two groups.

items: The conditions: six obligations fulfilled before starting the prayer.
The pillars: six obligations performed within the prayer.

sections.text: The work states that the prayer has twelve obligatory parts in total: six outside it and six within it.
If one of the conditions or pillars is missing, the prayer is not valid. This is why both groups need to be known.
Read the separate topics on the conditions and the pillars to complete your picture of these twelve.

articles.title: The necessary acts of the prayer
articles.summary: Acts ranking after the obligatory parts, whose omission calls for the prostration of forgetfulness.

sections.text: The necessary acts complete the obligatory ones. The work gives this measure: whoever performs a necessary act earns reward, and whoever omits one forgetfully must make the prostration of forgetfulness.

items: Beginning the prayer with the words 'Allahu akbar'.
Reciting Surah al-Fatiha in the prayer.
Reciting al-Fatiha in the first two units of obligatory prayers, and in every unit of witr and voluntary prayers.

sections.text: Whoever omits a necessary act deliberately must repeat the prayer.
This list summarises the principal necessary acts; the full list is given in more detail in the relevant section.
If you notice a slip during prayer, learning when the prostration of forgetfulness applies is a good starting point.

articles.title: The recommended acts of the prayer
articles.summary: Practices that beautify the prayer, whose omission does not invalidate it.

sections.text: The recommended acts complete the obligatory and necessary ones and beautify the prayer.
The work gives this ruling: omitting a recommended act in the prayer does not invalidate it and does not require the prostration of forgetfulness, though it is disliked.
This measure makes the difference clear: without an obligatory part the prayer is invalid, omitting a necessary act calls for redress, while recommended acts belong to completeness.
Learning the recommended acts turns the prayer from a hurried duty into an act performed with calm.
Begin by aiming to tell the obligatory, necessary and recommended acts apart.

articles.title: Praying in congregation
articles.summary: The reward of congregational prayer and its social benefits.

sections.text: Great importance is given to praying in congregation. Those who attend come to know one another, the less informed benefit from the more knowledgeable, and bonds of brotherhood and solidarity grow stronger.
According to the hadith cited in the work, the reward of the congregational prayer exceeds that of praying alone by twenty-seven degrees.
Congregation builds not only reward but a social bond: mutual affection and cooperation grow around the mosque.
Someone who cannot attend prays alone; this does not mean the prayer is invalid.
Trying one prayer a week in congregation can be a calm way to begin.

articles.title: Upon whom is fasting obligatory?
articles.summary: Three conditions make fasting obligatory; there is ease for the ill and the traveller.

sections.text: For fasting to become obligatory upon a person, certain conditions must be present.

items: Being Muslim.
Being of sound mind.
Having reached maturity.

sections.text: Even when these are present, those too ill to fast and those travelling may refrain; the ill make up the days once recovered, and travellers once they return.
Fasting is not obligatory on children who have not reached maturity, though accustoming them gradually, without harming them, is considered appropriate.
If you are unsure because of your health, you can consult both your doctor and a qualified religious official.

articles.title: What breaks the fast
articles.summary: Some things that break the fast require both a make-up day and expiation; others only a make-up day.

sections.text: Things that break the Ramadan fast fall into two groups by their consequence: some require both making up the day and expiation, others only making up the day.

items: Eating or drinking deliberately, without excuse, while knowing one is fasting.
Deliberate marital relations while knowing one is fasting.
Smoking, or drawing in the smoke of incense.

sections.text: The work counts the above among the cases requiring both a make-up day and expiation.
The work also explains when expiation is lifted: if the person becomes too ill to fast that same day, the expiation falls away, provided the illness was not self-induced.
If you have a doubt specific to your own case, consult a qualified religious official rather than deriving a ruling yourself.

articles.title: Upon whom is zakat obligatory?
articles.summary: Zakat becomes obligatory when conditions are met both in the owner and in the wealth.

sections.text: For a person to be liable for zakat, certain conditions must be present both in themselves and in the wealth they own.

items: Being Muslim.
Having reached maturity.
Being of sound mind.
Being free.
That the wealth remaining after debts is not below the threshold.

sections.text: The conditions in the wealth are: that it reaches the threshold, that it is of a growing nature, and that a lunar year has passed over it.
The work notes in parentheses that according to the Shafi'i school, zakat is also due on the wealth of children and those who lack legal capacity, this duty being carried out by their guardians.
The threshold is a measure of wealth set by the religion. Someone who owns this much beyond their debts and essential needs is considered religiously well-off.
Zakat calculation depends on personal finances; consulting a qualified authority is the soundest approach.

articles.differenceNote: Eserde, Şâfiîlere göre çocukların ve akıl hastalarının mallarından da zekât verilmesi gerektiği, bu görevi velilerinin yerine getireceği belirtilir.

articles.title: Who may receive zakat?
articles.summary: The recipients of zakat are specified in the Qur'an.

sections.text: Those to whom zakat may be given are specified in the Qur'an; the work bases its treatment on verse 60 of Surah at-Tawbah.
The categories of zakat recipients are listed in Surah at-Tawbah, verse 60 (see the Quran tab).

items: The poor: those whose wealth is below the threshold and who are not religiously counted as well-off.
The needy: those who possess nothing, in greater difficulty than the poor.
Debtors: those without wealth above the threshold beyond their debt, unable to repay it.

sections.text: The work explains each of these categories; zakat is not given at random but to the specified recipients.
When giving zakat it is enough to know which category the recipient falls into; further questioning is not required.

articles.title: Upon whom is hajj obligatory?
articles.summary: Hajj, performed with both wealth and body, is obligatory on those meeting certain conditions.

sections.text: Hajj, an act of worship performed with both wealth and body, is obligatory upon those who meet certain conditions.

items: Being Muslim.
Being of sound mind.
Having reached maturity.
Being free.
Having, beyond essential needs, the means to support oneself and one's dependants until returning.
Having the funds for the journey's costs.

sections.text: The work additionally lists separate conditions for performing hajj in person: being physically well, having no impediment such as imprisonment, and the route being safe.
Hajj is not obligatory upon someone who does not meet the conditions; this is not a shortcoming but an ease the religion observes.
If you intend to perform hajj, you might begin by calmly assessing the financial and health conditions.

articles.title: The qurban offering
articles.summary: Qurban is the sacrifice, with the intention of worship, of an animal meeting set conditions at a set time.

sections.text: Qurban is the sacrifice, with the intention of worship, of an animal bearing certain qualities at a specified time. It is called udhiyah.
Qurban is one of the financial acts of worship and is described as an expression of gratitude for the blessings granted.
The work notes that the practice is very old and that in its present form it goes back to the Prophet Ibrahim.
The timing, the qualities required in the animal, and upon whom it is incumbent each carry their own rulings, treated in detail in the relevant section.
If you are considering offering a qurban, begin by learning its time and the qualities required in the animal.

articles.title: What are hadith and sunnah?
articles.summary: Hadith refers to the sayings transmitted from the Prophet; sunnah refers to the way he lived. Both are core sources that explain the Qur'an.

sections.text: Hadith is the general name for the sayings transmitted from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Sunnah refers together to his words, his practice and his approvals. The two together show how the Qur'an was understood and how it was lived day to day.
Hadith and sunnah do not take the place of the Qur'an; they are core sources that help explain it and help us understand how it is applied in life.
Rereading and explaining hadith texts in every age is an effort to build a bridge between the text and lived life.

These narrations were transmitted carefully throughout history and in time grew into a very large body of literature. Hadith scholars worked both to transmit the texts faithfully and to keep the principles and values of the sunnah livable.
Classical hadith sources are not works that everyone can draw on easily. For this reason, in almost every period studies have been produced to make this accumulated knowledge accessible.
When you come across a hadith, first look at which subject it explains; learning its source and context is the first step to understanding it correctly.

articles.title: Knowledge and guidance: the parable of rain
articles.summary: The Prophet compared the knowledge and guidance sent with him to rain, and people to different kinds of soil that receive that rain differently.

sections.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) compared the guidance and knowledge God sent with him to abundant rain falling on soils of different kinds.

The comparison describes three cases. One soil absorbs the water and grows abundant plants. Another holds the water on its surface; people drink from it, water their animals and farm with it. The third is flat and bare: it neither holds water nor grows plants.
The heart of the comparison is this: what water is to soil, the guidance that comes through revelation is to a human being.

The source explains it this way: the person who learns and absorbs this knowledge and also teaches it to others is like fertile soil; the person who pays it no attention is like barren ground that does not accept water.
The measure here is not to judge people but to make us reflect on our own attitude toward knowledge. Sharing what you have learned is as much part of the comparison as learning it.
Share a useful piece of knowledge you learned from a source you trust, together with its correct context.

verification.sourceLocator: Hadislerle İslâm, Cilt 1, s. 397
verification.evidenceSummary: Sayfada, Allah Resûlü'nün kendisiyle gönderilen hidayet ve ilmi farklı topraklara düşen bol yağmura benzettiği rivayet ve ardından gelen açıklama yer alır; üç toprak türü sayılır.

articles.title: Compassion toward animals
articles.summary: The Prophet urged responsible treatment of animals that cannot speak, and opposed cruelty toward them and needless harm.

sections.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) urged those with him to carry a sense of responsibility toward animals, saying: "Fear God regarding these animals that cannot speak."

An incident recorded in the source makes this concrete. One day, travelling with his cousin Abdullah ibn Ja'far, the Messenger of God saw a camel tied in a date garden. When the camel saw him it began to groan and tears ran from its eyes. The Prophet went up to it and stroked its ears, and the animal grew calm.
He then called for the camel's owner and said to him: "Do you not fear God regarding this camel that He has given you? It has complained to me that you leave it hungry and work it to exhaustion."
The measure here is clear: a living creature in our care is a responsibility upon us.

The source notes that animals were created for people to benefit from, and that they are at the same time part of nature's beauty and a subject worth reflecting on. The Prophet himself came from within this life: like other prophets he herded sheep, and at times milked his animals with his own hands.

This compassion was not a feeling that stayed in words. According to the source the Prophet forbade taking living creatures as targets and setting animals to fight one another; he took measures to protect animal life, and opposed cruelty toward animals and needless harm to them.
Check today on the water, feed, shelter and rest of an animal that is in your care.

articles.title: Hilf al-Fudul: the pact of the virtuous
articles.summary: Formed in Mecca during the Prophet's youth, Hilf al-Fudul was a pact of solidarity aimed at standing beside anyone who suffered injustice.

sections.text: In pre-Islamic Arab society, disputes between individuals and tribes often turned into open conflict. This wore down trade, daily life and people's sense of security.

To overcome this, the tribes had accepted four months of the year as sacred (Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab) and pledged not to fight during them. Even so, wars were waged in the sacred months; these were called the Fijar wars.
In this climate, safety of life, property and honour in Mecca had grown badly weakened. Vulnerable people who came to the city to trade were subjected to injustice.
A merchant from Yemen who was in Mecca for trade could not obtain payment for the goods he had sold, and called out loudly for justice. That cry became the turning point.

The tribes who heard it gathered in a house and swore an oath that no one would be wronged and that anyone suffering injustice would be helped. The core of the oath was this: when someone in Mecca was wronged, whether that person was one of their own or a stranger, they would act as a single hand until the right was restored.
When you see an injustice around you, before saying "this is not my concern", recall the measure of this pact: what matters is not who was wronged, but the wrong itself.

verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, cahiliye Arap toplumundaki anlaşmazlıkları, haram ayları ve Ficâr savaşlarını anlatır; Mekke'de haksızlığa uğrayan Yemenli tüccarın feryadı üzerine kabilelerin toplanıp haksızlığa uğrayana yardım etme yemini ettiğini ve yeminin içeriğini aktarır.

articles.title: The arbitration at the Kaaba
articles.summary: A dispute that arose during the repair of the Kaaba, and was close to turning into fighting, ended with a simple and fair solution the Prophet proposed.

sections.text: The Kaaba is the first place of worship on earth, built by God's command by Abraham and his son Ishmael. Even before Islam it was regarded as an important religious centre.

In the year 605 CE, when the Prophet was around thirty-five, the Quraysh decided to repair the Kaaba. The building had been worn down by fire and flood damage. All the Quraysh clans drew lots to divide the work, and each contributed a set share.

Those who would contribute financially were told that the money given for the Kaaba must be clean and lawfully earned, and that nothing obtained through usury or injustice should be mixed into the work. The Prophet himself took part in the repair, carrying stones together with his uncle Abbas.

When the building was finished, a dispute arose over who would set the Black Stone in its place. No clan was willing to leave the task to another; the argument lasted for days and some were even ready to fight over it.

In the end they agreed on a proposal: "Let us make the first person to enter the Kaaba through the gate of Banu Shayba our arbitrator." When the Prophet came through the gate, the Quraysh expressed their relief, saying "Here comes al-Amin."

Accepted as arbitrator, the Prophet called for a cloth, placed the Black Stone on it with his own hands, and asked the chiefs of every clan to take hold of an edge. When the stone reached the required height he lifted it himself and set it in place. In this way a serious conflict that was about to break out was prevented by a solution everyone accepted.
In a disagreement, think through a solution that is both fair and brings all sides into the process.

verification.sourceLocator: Hz. Muhammed'in Hayatı (16. Baskı, 2025), Kâbe Hakemliği, s. 47-50
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, Kâbe'nin Hz. İbrahim ve Hz. İsmail tarafından inşa edilen ilk mescit oluşunu; miladî 605'te Kureyş'in Kâbe'yi tamir kararını; Hacerülesved'i yerine koyma tartışmasını ve Peygamberimizin örtü çözümüyle çatışmayı önlemesini anlatır.

articles.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and Sermon
articles.summary: The address the Prophet gave at Arafat during the last pilgrimage of his life reads as a farewell that sums up basic rights and responsibilities.

sections.text: In the tenth year after the migration (632) the Prophet began preparing to perform the pilgrimage and asked all Muslims to join the journey. He set out from Medina, entered the state of consecration at Dhu al-Hulayfa, and reached Mecca.
On Friday the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah he moved on to Arafat. After combining the noon and afternoon prayers, he delivered to a very large gathering at Arafat the address known as the Farewell Sermon.

He began by reminding everyone that all people are servants of God and descend from the same parents. He stated that people are equal regardless of race, colour, language or class, and that the measure of excellence in God's sight is mindfulness of Him.
The sermon dwells largely on human rights: the safety of life, property and honour, care for the rights owed to others, avoiding oppression and unlawful gain, and keeping trusts.

The Prophet asked that mutual rights and responsibilities between spouses be observed, and drew attention to unity by declaring that all Muslims are brothers and sisters. He said the Qur'an and the Sunnah are indispensable guidance, and stressed performing acts of worship such as prayer, fasting, zakat and pilgrimage, and keeping to moral principles.

He announced that certain practices of the pre-Islamic era were abolished, and that usury and blood vengeance were forbidden. Throughout the address he repeatedly asked those present, "Have I conveyed the message?", having them affirm what he said, and closed by saying three times, "Bear witness, O Lord!"
Think of one small step you can take today to protect what is owed to another person.

verification.sourceLocator: Hz. Muhammed'in Hayatı (16. Baskı, 2025), Veda Haccı ve Hutbesi, s. 248-251
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, hicretin 10. yılındaki hac yolculuğunu tarihleriyle anlatır ve Arafat'ta yapılan Veda Hutbesi'nin içeriğini özetler: insanların eşitliği, üstünlük ölçüsünün takvâ oluşu, can/mal/ırz güvenliği, kul hakkı, emanet, eşlerin karşılıklı hakları, kardeşlik, Kur'an ve Sünnet'e bağlılık, faizin ve kan davasının kaldırılması. articles.title: Who is a prophet?
articles.summary: A prophet is a chosen human being appointed by God to show people the right path, acting as a messenger between God and His servants.

sections.text: One of the six articles of faith is believing in the prophets.

The word used in Turkish for prophet, "peygamber", comes from Persian and means "one who carries news". In religious terms it refers to a chosen human being whom God appoints to show people the right path. A prophet announces to people what God has revealed to him, acting as a messenger between God and His servants.

According to the explanation in the Diyanet İslam İlmihali, a scripture was sent down to some of the prophets; these are called "rasul". To others no scripture was sent down; they act upon the scriptures revealed to prophets before them and convey those scriptures. These are called "nabi".
By the definition given in that same source, every rasul is also a nabi, but not every nabi is a rasul.

People need prophets, because a human being cannot know everything by reason alone. Even if we can reach God, who created us and the universe, through our reason, we cannot work out on our own how to worship Him or what His commands and prohibitions are. It is the prophets who make these known to us.
The next time you hear the words "rasul" and "nabi", recall the difference between them; this distinction is the key to understanding prophethood.

verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, peygamber kelimesinin Farsça 'haber götüren' anlamını, dindeki tanımını, resul-nebi ayrımını ve insanın peygambere olan ihtiyacını açıklar.

articles.title: The attributes of the prophets
articles.summary: So that they could carry out the task of conveying God's message, the prophets bear the attributes of truthfulness, trustworthiness, conveyance, intelligence and protection from sin.

sections.text: Since the prophets act as messengers between God and His servants, their task is to make God known, to teach how He is to be worshipped, and to announce His commands and prohibitions. All the prophets fulfilled this task completely.

The prophets are human beings like us. Yet because they are God's chosen servants they have certain attributes. These fall into two groups, necessary and permissible. In the source, the attributes regarded as necessarily present in the prophets are called the "necessary attributes".

There are five necessary attributes. Truthfulness (sidq): the prophets never lie, and do not deceive or act unjustly. Trustworthiness (amana): being reliable. Conveyance (tabligh): announcing in full everything revealed to them. Intelligence (fatana): being wise and discerning, for without it they could not carry out their task. Protection from sin (isma): being kept from sin.
These five attributes explain the trustworthiness of the prophets in the task of conveying the message.
The permissible attributes are qualities found in other people as well: because the prophets too are human, they eat, drink, sleep, grow tired, and when their lifetime ends they pass away.
Reflect briefly on truthfulness and trustworthiness: where do keeping your word and guarding what is entrusted to you come up for you today?

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Peygamberlere İman, s. 60-61
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, peygamberlerin görevlerini ve kendilerinde bulunması vacib olan beş sıfatı (sıdk, emanet, tebliğ, fetanet, ismet) tanımlar; ayrıca peygamberlerin insan olmaları yönüyle taşıdıkları caiz sıfatları açıklar.

articles.title: The prophets named in the Qur'an
articles.summary: Twenty-five prophets are named in the Qur'an; the number of all the prophets God sent is known to God alone.

sections.text: Between the first prophet, Adam, and the last prophet, Muhammad (peace be upon him), many prophets came and passed.
Only God knows their exact number. The Qur'an gives the names of some prophets and states that there were many more whose names are not given.
For this reason a Muslim believes in all the prophets God sent and leaves their number to God.

Twenty-five prophets are named in the Qur'an: Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Ibrahim, Lut, Ishaq, Isma'il, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Dhul-Kifl, Ilyas, Al-Yasa', Zakariya, Yunus, Yahya, Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them).
Believing in the prophets requires believing not only in some of them, but in all the prophets God sent.
Note down a name you do not recognise, and set it aside to learn about from a source you trust.

verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, ilk peygamber Hz. Âdem ile son peygamber Hz. İhtilaflı sınıflandırmalar bu makaleye ALINMAMIŞTIR.

articles.title: What is dua?
articles.summary: Dua is the servant turning to their Lord and laying their need before Him; the source calls it "the essence of servanthood".

sections.text: Dua is the servant turning to their Lord, asking of Him and laying their need before Him. The source describes dua as "the essence of servanthood".
The Qur'an says: "Call upon Me, and I will respond to you." This call is a reminder that a servant is always invited to turn to their Lord.
According to the source, it is through dua that a servant holds worth in God's sight.
This meaning is expressed in the verse: "Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your prayer." Dua is the name of the bond a person forms with their Lord.
Seen this way, dua is not merely asking for something; it is recognising one's own helplessness and need, and turning to one's Lord in trust.
Say something to your Lord today in your own plain words; you do not need to know a special formula to make dua.

verification.sourceLocator: Hadislerle İslâm, Cilt 2, Dua: Kulluğun Özü, s. 40

articles.title: The importance of family
articles.summary: The family is the nucleus of society and a person's first place of learning; its peace is kept when its members carry their responsibilities toward one another.

sections.text: A family is made up of mother, father and children. The source describes the family as the nucleus of society and the foundation stone of a nation: the larger community called a nation is formed by families coming together.
Just as a building is sound only if the parts that make it up are sound, a society is strong only if the families that make it up are sound.
The family is a school in which the first knowledge of faith and character is given and spiritual values are taught.

According to the source, the ease and peace sought in this home can only be secured when family members fulfil their duties toward one another. This is why it matters that each person knows the responsibility they carry.
The continuity of the family is fundamental; the source asks that words and behaviour which would cause a family to break apart be avoided.
Say one kind word today to a member of your family, without asking anything of them.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Ailemize Karşı Görevlerimiz — Ailenin Önemi, s. 503
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, ailenin ana, baba ve çocuklardan oluştuğunu, toplumun çekirdeği olduğunu; dinî ve ahlaki ilk bilgilerin verildiği bir okul durumunda bulunduğunu; huzurun ancak fertlerin birbirine karşı görevlerini yerine getirmesiyle sağlanabileceğini belirtir.

articles.title: Respect and kindness toward parents
articles.summary: The heart of how we treat our parents is courtesy: gentle words, conduct that does not wound, and a respectful tone of voice.

sections.text: The source lists the duties owed to parents as plain items. The first of them is to be cheerful and gentle-spoken toward them.
The second measure is in the look: not to gaze at them harshly or in anger. The third is in speech and conduct — not to wound them in any way.
The source conveys this delicacy through a striking limit: not to say even "uff" to them.
The same passage also lists not raising one's voice in their presence. What these items share is the tone of communication with parents: gentle words and a respectful manner.
The source counts a duty toward parents who have died as well: to remember them with mercy.
Pay attention to your tone of voice when you speak with a parent today; if they have passed away, remember them kindly.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Anne ve Babamıza Karşı Görevlerimiz, s. 507-508
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, anne babaya karşı görevleri maddeler hâlinde sayar: güler yüzlü ve tatlı dilli olmak, yüzlerine sert ve öfkeli bakmamak, söz ve davranışla hiçbir şekilde incitmemek ("öf" bile dememek), yanlarında yüksek sesle konuşmamak; vefatlarından sonra ise onları rahmetle anmak.

articles.title: The concepts of halal and haram
articles.summary: According to the Diyanet İslam İlmihali, halal is what is not religiously forbidden and haram is what is definitively forbidden. The default is permissibility.

sections.text: According to the definition in the Diyanet İslam İlmihali, halal means that which it is not religiously forbidden to do, eat or drink. Haram is that which is definitively forbidden in religion.
Accordingly, if something is halal it is not haram, and if it is haram it cannot be halal.
By the same source, the default is permissibility: nothing is forbidden except what has been declared so, and the things made haram are countable and limited.
The source completes this measure with a warning from the Qur'an: "Do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful'."

This warning shows that it is not right to issue rulings of halal or haram without knowledge, on our own opinion. When your own situation requires a definitive ruling, you should turn to the competent official authority.
When you hesitate over whether something is permissible, ask a trustworthy and competent source instead of guessing.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Helaller ve Haramlar, s. 383-384
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm helal ve haramı tanımlar; Allah'ın yarattığı her şeyde aslolanın helal ve mübah olduğunu, haram kılınanların sayılı ve sınırlı olduğunu belirtir; ve "Dillerinizin yalan olarak nitelediği şeyler hakkında 'Bu helaldir, bu da haramdır' demeyin" ayetini aktararak bilgisizce helal-haram hükmü vermeyi men eder.

articles.title: What does the hereafter mean?
articles.summary: The hereafter is the life that begins with resurrection and continues forever; belief in it is one of the six articles of faith.

sections.text: One of the six articles of faith is believing in the hereafter.
The source begins with a simple measure: everything other than God has an end. The world too will one day come to an end. The only one who will never die and will remain is God.
The time that begins with resurrection and continues forever is called the Day of the Hereafter.
According to the source, after the end of the world the trumpet will be sounded a second time and all creatures will be raised again. This is called resurrection after death.
To those who say "we cannot grasp being raised after death", the source gives a plain answer: the God who created us when we were nothing is also able to raise us again.
Believing in the Day of the Hereafter means believing in these things.
Think of belief in the hereafter not as a list of fears, but as a measure reminding you that life has an end and a reckoning.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Ahirete İman — Ahiret Ne Demektir? / Öldükten Sonra Dirilmek, s. 65-67
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, ahirete imanın imanın altı şartından biri olduğunu; Allah'tan başka her şeyin bir sonu bulunduğunu ve yalnız Allah'ın bâki olduğunu; sûra ikinci üfürüşle bütün yaratıkların yeniden dirileceğini; bu dirilişle başlayıp sonsuza kadar devam edecek zamana "Ahiret Günü" dendiğini ve ahiret gününe iman etmenin bunlara inanmak olduğunu belirtir.

articles.title: The time of the Hour is unknown
articles.summary: That the Hour will come is certain; but no one except God knows when — and the Prophet said he had no knowledge of it either.

sections.text: The source carefully separates two things: that the Hour will come is certain, but when it will come is not known.
No one except God knows the time of the Hour; the source records that the Prophet too said he had no knowledge of it.
This measure leads to a plain conclusion: predictions about the date of the Hour have no religious basis. Speaking as though we know a time we do not know does not fit what the source says.
What is known for certain, according to the source, is that one day the order of the heavens and the earth will break down and the whole universe will come to an end; its timing rests with God.
When you meet a claim about a date or a sign of the Hour, recall the measure the source sets: only God knows its time.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Ahirete İman — Kıyamet Ne Zaman Kopacaktır?, s. 66
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, kıyametin kopacağının muhakkak olmakla birlikte zamanını Allah'tan başka kimsenin bilemeyeceğini ve Peygamberimizin de bu hususta bilgisi olmadığını söylediğini açıkça belirtir.

articles.title: How belief in the hereafter shapes life
articles.summary: Belief in the hereafter is not an abstract acceptance; according to the source it directly shapes conduct, relationships and intention.

sections.text: The source explains the effect of belief in the hereafter through conduct: a person who believes they will be raised again one day and will answer for what they did listens to God's commands and keeps away from what He forbade.
This belief becomes visible in character. According to the source, such a person takes care to acquire good character and treats their relatives and neighbours well.
The same measure appears in dealings with others: they keep away from deceit, injustice and cheating, and try to do good to everyone as far as they can.
The source does not stop at visible behaviour: it recalls that a person will be asked not only about what they did, but also about what they kept hidden within.
For this reason belief in the hereafter calls for more than appearing proper on the outside; it calls for clearing the heart of bad feelings as well.
Check your intention once while doing something today: as much as the visible act, what lies behind it is part of this measure.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), Ahirete İman — Ahirete İmanın Faydaları, s. 67
verification.evidenceSummary: Bölüm, ahirete inanan kimsenin Allah'ın emirlerini dinleyip yasaklarından sakındığını, güzel ahlakla ahlaklanmaya özen gösterdiğini, akraba ve komşularına iyi davrandığını, hile, haksızlık ve aldatmadan sakındığını, elinden geldiğince iyilik yapmaya çalıştığını; ayrıca yalnız yaptıklarından değil içinde sakladıklarından da sorulacağına inandığı için kalbini kötü duygulardan arındırmaya çalıştığını belirtir.

articles.title: Women asking to learn
articles.summary: After a woman voiced her request to learn, the Prophet set aside a separate day for women and taught them himself.

sections.text: A narration recorded in the source shows women's request to learn in their own words. A woman came to the Prophet and said: "Men benefit from your teaching all the time; set aside a day for us too, so we may come to you and you may teach us from what God has taught you."
The Prophet did not turn the request away; he said: "Then gather on such and such days."
The women gathered on the appointed day, and the Messenger of God came to them and taught them from what God had taught him.

The source does not leave this example standing alone. The same passage relates that in that period women were aware of their social rights and duties, and took part in areas such as seeking knowledge, trade, solidarity and mutual help, and caring for the sick.
The measure here is plain: a request to learn was voiced, it was met, and it was given a regular arrangement.
If there is something you want to learn, say it plainly instead of putting the question off; in this narration too, everything began with a question.

articles.title: The writing and copying of the Qur'an
articles.summary: From the time of its revelation the Qur'an was preserved both by memorisation and in writing; it was later gathered into a single mushaf and copied for the main centres.

sections.text: The revealed verses were being memorised on the one hand and, by the Prophet's instruction, written down by the scribes of revelation on the other.

There was no paper at that time. According to the source, the verses were written on thin stones, shoulder blades, palm branches and hides. The Prophet would read the verses and have the scribes read them back, to check that what was written was correct.
In this way the Qur'an was preserved in the Prophet's own lifetime, both in writing and in memory.

In the period of Abu Bakr, after around seventy memorisers were killed at Yamama, a commission was formed under Zayd ibn Thabit, who had served as a scribe of revelation. Drawing both on what the scribes had written and on the memories of those who had memorised it, this commission gathered the Qur'an with great care into a single mushaf.

In the period of Uthman, when differences in recitation began to appear in different regions, a commission again headed by Zayd ibn Thabit took the original copy kept with Hafsa and produced some seven copies. These were sent to various Islamic centres, and mistaken readings were thereby prevented.
The source also notes that some copies written in that period have reached our own day.
When you look at the mushaf in your hands, recall once how this text was preserved and passed on through writing and memorisation.

articles.title: What is a madhhab?
articles.summary: "Madhhab" literally means "a road travelled". According to the source, the madhhabs arose from differences of interpretation among scholars on matters with no clear and decisive text; all of them take the Quran and the Sunnah as their basis.

sections.text: In the İslam İlmihali, "madhhab" is explained literally as "a road travelled". As a term it is defined as "the views of a religion that arise from differences of interpretation among its scholars".
The source states that madhhabs exist in Islam, that there is no difference between them in fundamentals, and that all of them take the Quran and the Sunnah of the Prophet as their basis.
Madhhabs are described not as bodies that diverge on the fundamentals of the religion, but as differences of interpretation resting on those same two sources.

According to the source, the difference arises on matters where there is no clear and decisive text (a verse or a hadith). On such matters scholars performed ijtihad and stated their views. Scholars qualified to perform ijtihad may reach the same view on a question, or they may state different views.
The İslam İlmihali treats madhhabs under two headings: those of belief and those of practice. This article is limited to the definition of the concept.
This article is not advice on choosing a madhhab. A reader who needs a ruling for their own situation should consult the competent official authority.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), İtikad — II. İslâm'da Mezhepler / A) Mezhep Nedir?, s. 29
verification.evidenceSummary: s. 29, "A) Mezhep Nedir?" başlığı altında mezhebi sözlükte "gidilen yol", terim olarak "bir dinin, bilginleri arasındaki yorum farklarından meydana gelen görüşleri" diye tanımlar. Aynı sayfa, İslam dininde mezheplerin bulunduğunu, bunlar arasında temelde bir ayrılık olmadığını ve hepsinin Kur'an-ı Kerim'i ve Peygamberimizin sünnetini esas aldığını belirtir. Farklılığın kaynağı olarak, hakkında açık ve kesin nass bulunmayan hususlarda bilginlerin ictihad edip görüş bildirmesi gösterilir; ictihad yetkisi olan bilginlerin aynı görüşe varabilecekleri gibi farklı görüşler de belirtebilecekleri söylenir. Sayfa, mezheplerin itikadî ve amelî olmak üzere ikiye ayrıldığını da kaydeder.

articles.title: The primary sources of religious rulings
articles.summary: The İslam İlmihali lists four sources on which religious rulings rest: the Book, the Sunnah, ijma and qiyas. According to the source the Book and the Sunnah are the principal sources; ijma and qiyas rest upon these two.

sections.text: The İslam İlmihali lists four sources on which religious rulings rest: the Book, the Sunnah, ijma and qiyas.

The Book is the Quran. The source defines it as "the speech sent down to our Prophet in Arabic through Gabriel, transmitted to us by mass transmission and written in the mushafs", and states that the Quran is the first source on which religious rulings rest.

"Sunnah" literally means "way and custom". As a term it is the sayings and actions of the Prophet other than the Quran. The source divides it in three: verbal sunnah (his sayings), practical sunnah (his actions) and tacit sunnah — his remaining silent rather than objecting to something he was aware of.

"Ijma" literally means agreeing on a matter. According to the source, in religion it means the agreement of Muslim scholars, in some period after the Prophet, on the ruling of a religious question. Agreement stated openly is called explicit ijma; the silence of other qualified scholars who knew of a view and did not object is called tacit ijma.

The source openly records a difference of opinion here: according to the great majority of Muslim scholars explicit ijma is a decisive source for religious rulings, whereas whether tacit ijma is decisive is disputed.

"Qiyas" literally means measuring one thing against another. In religion it means giving a question that has no ruling in the Book, the Sunnah or ijma the ruling of a case found in one of those sources, because of a shared underlying cause.
According to the source the first two of these four — the Book and the Sunnah — are the principal sources in religion, while ijma and qiyas go back to the Book and the Sunnah.
This article only conveys the definitions of these sources. It does not explain each madhhab's own method, does not compare madhhabs and does not give a ruling on any question.

verification.sourceLocator: İslam İlmihali (34. Baskı, 2019), İtikad — III. Dinî Hükümlerin Kaynakları (Şer'î Deliller), s. 33-38
verification.evidenceSummary: s. 33'teki "Dinî Hükümlerin Kaynakları (Şer'î Deliller)" başlığı, hükümlerin dayandığı kaynakların Kitap, Sünnet, İcma ve Kıyas olmak üzere dört olduğunu söyler ve Kitap'ı Kur'an-ı Kerim diye tanımlayıp ilk kaynak olduğunu belirtir. s. 34 sünneti sözlükte "yol ve âdet", terim olarak Peygamberimizin Kur'an'dan başka söz ve davranışları diye tanımlar ve kavlî, fiilî, takrirî üçlü ayrımını verir. s. 36-37 icmayı tanımlar, sarih ve sükûtî icma ayrımını yapar ve çoğunluğa göre sarih icmanın kesin, sükûtî icmanın kesinliğinin ise tartışmalı olduğunu kaydeder. s. 37 kıyası tanımlar. s. 38, Kitap ve Sünnetin dinde asıl kaynaklar olduğunu, İcma ve Kıyasın bunlara raci olduğunu belirtir.

articles.title: The schools of law in practice
articles.summary: The İslam İlmihali lists the schools of law widespread among Sunni Muslims as Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali. This article only introduces them; it neither compares nor ranks them.

sections.text: Under the heading "schools of law in practice", the İslam İlmihali lists four schools widespread among Sunni Muslims: Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali.
The source introduces these four as those "widespread among Sunni Muslims". This is not a ranking of merit, and it carries no judgement about scholarly traditions not mentioned here.

The founder of the Hanafi school is Abu Hanifa, known as Imam A'zam; his name was Nu'man and his father's name Thabit. According to the source he was born in Kufa in AH 80 (CE 699) and died in AH 150 (CE 767). His school spread first in Iraq, then in Egypt, India and the Turkish lands.

The founder of the Maliki school is Imam Malik b. Anas. He was born in Medina in AH 93 (CE 712) and died there in AH 179 (CE 795). His principal work is al-Muwatta. The school emerged in Medina and spread in the Hijaz, Africa and Andalusia.

The founder of the Shafi'i school is Imam Muhammad b. Idris al-Shafi'i. He was born in Gaza in AH 150 (CE 767) and died in Egypt in AH 204 (CE 819). The school spread in Egypt, southern Arabia, East Africa, Azerbaijan, Eastern Anatolia, Indonesia and Java.

The founder of the Hanbali school is Ahmad b. Hanbal. He was born in Baghdad in AH 164 (CE 780) and died there in AH 241 (CE 855). He is known for his hadith work, the Musnad. The school spread in Baghdad, Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz.
This article is introductory. It does not compare the legal differences between the schools, does not hold one above another, and does not tell the reader which school to follow.

verification.evidenceSummary: s. 31'deki "2. Amelde Mezhepler" başlığı, "Sünni Müslümanlar arasında yaygın amelde mezhepler Hanefi, Şafii, Maliki ve Hanbeli olmak üzere dörttür" der. articles.title: What is the Hijri calendar?
articles.summary: According to the explanation on the Presidency of Religious Affairs' Vakit Hesaplama page, the Hijri calendar is a calendar system that takes the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina as its starting point and is based on the Moon's orbit around the Earth.

sections.text: According to the explanation on the Presidency of Religious Affairs' Vakit Hesaplama page, the Hijri calendar is a calendar system that takes the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina as its starting point and is based on the Moon's orbit around the Earth.
The source divides the Hijri calendar in two: the Hijri solar and the Hijri lunar calendar. The one commonly known simply as "the Hijri calendar" is the lunar one.

According to the source, the Hijri solar calendar is based on the Earth's orbit around the Sun, while the Hijri lunar calendar rests on the movement of the Moon. The two systems also have different starting days.
The Hijri calendar is a dating system. Bismillah only introduces it; it does not determine the official date of any religious day.

articles.title: Hijri months and the length of the year
articles.summary: In the Hijri lunar calendar twelve months follow a fixed order, and months have 29 or 30 days. Because the lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the Gregorian year, the Hijri year begins 10-11 days earlier each year.

sections.text: According to the source, the months of the Hijri lunar calendar follow this order: Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi al-Akhir, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhira, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja.
Months have sometimes 29 and sometimes 30 days.

A lunar year is 354 days. The source notes that the Hijri calendar also has leap years: within each 30-year period the 2nd, 5th, 7th, 10th, 13th, 15th, 18th, 21st, 24th, 26th and 29th years have 355 days, and the remaining years 354.
A lunar year is 354.367 days and a Gregorian year 365.2422 days. Because of this difference of roughly 10.9 days, the Hijri year begins 10-11 days earlier than the Gregorian year each year.
This shift is a natural consequence of the calendar system. It carries no meaning of fortune, prediction or superiority.

verification.evidenceSummary: Sayfa ayları sırasıyla Muharrem, Safer, Rebiülevvel, Rebiülahir, Cemaziyelevvel, Cemaziyelahir, Recep, Şaban, Ramazan, Şevval, Zilkade ve Zilhicce olarak verir. articles.title: The starting point of the Hijri calendar
articles.summary: According to the source, before Islam each important event served as a separate dating epoch. By a decision taken in the time of Umar, the year of the migration became the first year of the Hijri calendar and Muharram its first month.

sections.text: According to the source, before Islam each important event was taken as a dating epoch; the Year of the Elephant was the last such starting point. Counting years separately by each important event caused confusion.

Hz. Muhammed'in Hayatı describes the same situation: the Arabs of that period used no fixed calendar and dated events as "in the Year of the Elephant", "before the Year of the Elephant" or "after the Year of the Elephant".

By a decision taken in the time of Umar, in the seventeenth year after the migration, the year in which the migration took place was accepted as the first year of the Hijri calendar, and the month of Muharram of that year as the start of the year.
The source also records that the Hijri lunar and Hijri solar calendars have different starting days.
This article explains the calendar's starting point. It does not enter into the political disputes of that period and does not settle any question of chronology.
